content.title: About
content.content: Cauliflower is a cruciferous vegetable derived from the inflorescence of Brassica oleracea var. botrytis. When boiled in water without added salt (NS – no salt) it retains most of its vitamins and minerals, has a tender texture and a mild flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “cauliflower” comes from the resemblance of the curd to small flowers.
There are several varieties: white, green (broccoflower) and purple, distinguished by pigment content.
In Japan it is often used as a low‑carb “rice” substitute, finely grated into rice‑like granules.
Cauliflower is rich in glucosinolates, which break down into compounds with anti‑cancer properties.
During World War II it was frequently used as a potato substitute in Europe due to shortages.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: One serving of cooked cauliflower provides over 70 % of the daily recommended vitamin C, supporting immune function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: 100 g of boiled cauliflower contains about 25 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight management.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Cauliflower contains raffinose, which can cause bloating and gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Interaction with medication
items.content: High vitamin K levels may affect the efficacy of anticoagulants such as warfarin.

items.title: Possible contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth; always use fresh heads.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked cauliflower can be served as a side dish, added to soups, purees, salads, or baked with cheese. For extra flavor, drizzle with olive oil, lemon juice, or sprinkle herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh cauliflower in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a perforated bag, for up to 5 days. Store cooked cauliflower in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3 days.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese, made with margarine

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled eggs with cheese, cooked in margarine. The dish was popular in the 1980s, combining the delicate flavor of eggs, the creamy aroma of cheese, and a hint of margarine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In the 1980s margarine was often used instead of butter because it was cheaper.
Cheese is usually a semi‑hard variety such as cheddar or gouda to melt evenly.
Eggs used for the omelet are typically fresh, though pasteurized eggs are also acceptable.
The dish cooks quickly, usually 5‑7 minutes in a pan.
Soviet cookbooks from the 1980s often recommend adding herbs for extra flavor.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs provide high‑quality complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply B12, riboflavin and biotin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Vitamin D source
items.content: Egg yolk offers a modest amount of vitamin D, aiding calcium absorption.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of fats and proteins provides quick satiety and energy.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs or cheese.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Margarine and cheese add saturated fats, so the dish should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should limit portion size.

items.title: Trans fats in margarine
items.content: Certain margarines may contain trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat eggs with a splash of milk, stir in grated cheese, salt and pepper. Melt margarine in a hot skillet, pour in the egg mixture and cook, stirring, until desired consistency is reached. Serve hot, optionally garnished with herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1‑2 days. Reheat in a pan or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg omelet with tomatoes is a simple dish made from beaten eggs, diced tomatoes, and a pinch of salt and pepper. The mixture is poured into a hot pan and cooked until lightly golden. It provides a good source of protein and vitamins while keeping fat content modest.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Omelets are among the quickest and most nutritious breakfast options.
Tomatoes increase the lycopene content, a powerful antioxidant.
Eggs contain all essential amino acids, making them a complete protein source.
Traditionally omelets are cooked in butter, but oil or non‑stick pans reduce added fat.
Around the world omelets are customized with cheese, herbs, ham, and other ingredients.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs supply complete protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Eggs provide B2, B6, and B12, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes add lycopene, which promotes heart health and has anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: When cooked with minimal oil, the omelet remains a low‑fat protein source.

items.title: Eye health support
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk help protect eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor intake.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor Salmonella; ensure the omelet is fully set before serving.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat eggs with a pinch of salt and pepper, stir in diced tomatoes. Heat a small amount of oil in a skillet over medium heat, pour in the mixture, and gently lift the edges as it sets. Cook until the omelet is firm but still moist, then slide onto a plate and serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours and reheat thoroughly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Fry sauce is a popular American condiment that blends the flavors of tomato ketchup and mayonnaise. It is commonly served with french fries, chicken nuggets, and other fried foods. The sauce has a creamy texture with a mildly sweet and slightly tangy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fry sauce originated in the United States in the 1950s and quickly became a fast‑food favorite.
The classic recipe includes tomato paste, mayonnaise, vinegar, sugar, and spices such as paprika and garlic.
In different regions the sauce has various names: in Utah it is called “fry sauce,” while in parts of the Midwest it is known as “red mayo.”
Home cooks often experiment with fry sauce as a chicken marinade or a base for barbecue sauces.
Its popularity surged in the 2020s thanks to social media where users share homemade versions.

items.title: Source of Vitamin A
items.content: Tomato ingredients provide beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, supporting vision.

items.title: Contains Vitamin E
items.content: The mayonnaise component supplies vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides Healthy Fats
items.content: Mayonnaise contains monounsaturated fats that can be heart‑friendly when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Rich in Lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes are high in lycopene, a compound linked to reduced risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Enhances Satiety
items.content: The balance of sweet, sour, and salty flavors can make meals more satisfying, potentially helping control overall calorie intake.

items.title: High Calorie Content
items.content: The combination of mayonnaise and sugar makes the sauce calorie‑dense; large portions may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Sugar and Salt Levels
items.content: Excessive sugar and salt can affect blood glucose and blood pressure.

items.title: Egg Allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise is typically made with egg yolks, making the sauce unsuitable for people with egg allergies.

items.title: Preservatives in Commercial Versions
items.content: Some store‑bought sauces contain artificial preservatives and stabilizers that may cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fry sauce with french fries, chicken nuggets, fish sticks, burgers, or as a dip for vegetable sticks. It can also be spread on sandwiches, added to salads, or used as a base for more complex sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sauce refrigerated in a sealed container. After opening, use within 1‑2 weeks. Discard if the smell, color, or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: The cheese muffin is a soft baked good made from wheat flour, eggs, milk, and grated cheese. It has a gentle aroma, a slightly sweet dough flavor, and a pronounced cheesy note. Suitable as a snack or as part of breakfast or lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese keeps the muffin moist and aromatic.
Traditionally cheddar is used, but any semi‑hard cheese works.
In the United States savory cheese muffins are a common café snack.
Herbs such as basil or dill are often added for extra flavor.
Muffins freeze well and can be reheated quickly in a microwave.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Cheese provides a substantial amount of complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Cheese is rich in calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the dough and cheese contain B1, B2 and B12 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour adds fiber, which aids digestion.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates and fats gives a quick source of energy.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: The cheese and butter in the batter make the muffin calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Cheese is often salty, which may be a concern for those with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making it unsuitable for gluten‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese muffins can be enjoyed warm or at room temperature. They are convenient for on‑the‑go eating, can be split and used as a base for a sandwich with ham or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze; reheat in the oven or microwave before serving.

nutritional-drink-or-shake-ready-to-drin.title: Nutritional drink or shake, ready-to-drink (Boost Plus)

content.title: About
content.content: Boost Plus is a ready‑to‑drink nutritional beverage/shake designed to support daily energy levels and post‑exercise recovery. The product provides a balanced blend of proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals, and performance‑enhancing ingredients such as creatine and BCAA to accelerate muscle repair.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Boost Plus is manufactured in the USA in GMP‑certified facilities.
Each 330 ml serving delivers approximately 250 kcal and 20 g of protein.
It contains 5 g of plant‑based protein, 3 g of fiber, and 30 mg of caffeine from natural guarana extract.
The formula is free from lactose, gluten, and artificial colorants.
The packaging is fully recyclable and aligns with sustainability principles.

items.title: Supports muscle recovery
items.content: A mix of fast‑ and slow‑digesting proteins together with BCAA promotes muscle protein synthesis after workouts.

items.title: Boosts energy
items.content: Caffeine and taurine help increase alertness and reduce feelings of fatigue.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: B‑vitamins, vitamin C and zinc contribute to normal immune system function.

items.title: Digestive regulation
items.content: Inulin fiber supports gut health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium) help maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Individuals sensitive to caffeine may experience nervousness, rapid heartbeat, or sleep disturbances.

items.title: Protein allergy
items.content: Contains plant proteins (soy, pea); avoid if you have known allergies.

items.title: Sugar intake
items.content: Although sugar content is modest, people with diabetes should account for the carbs and calories.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Caffeine can potentiate certain stimulants; consult a healthcare professional if you take medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Consume one bottle (330 ml) immediately after training or as a meal replacement breakfast. The drink is ready to drink, but you may chill it or add ice if desired. Do not mix with alcohol.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 48 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Spanakopita is a traditional Greek pastry made from layers of phyllo dough filled with a mixture of spinach, feta cheese, onions, herbs, and sometimes eggs. The dough becomes crisp and golden when baked. It is enjoyed as a snack, light meal, or part of a festive spread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spanakopita has been known in Greece since the 19th century, though its ancestors appear in Ottoman cuisine.
The classic recipe uses only feta, but modern versions may include ricotta, mozzarella, or even seafood.
Phyllo dough is so thin it is often called "paper" dough, and mastering its handling is considered an art.
In some Greek regions the pastry is served with a yogurt‑lemon sauce or a drizzle of fresh lemon juice.
It is frequently prepared as bite‑size triangles, perfect for buffet service.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Spinach, the main filling, provides iron, essential for blood formation.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Calcium from feta
items.content: Feta adds calcium, important for strong teeth and bones.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with modest oil, spanakopita remains a relatively light snack.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Spinach is rich in lutein and beta‑carotene, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Feta may trigger allergic reactions in people sensitive to milk proteins or lactose.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Traditional feta is salty, so the dish can be high in sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates that can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve spanakopita warm or hot, cut into serving pieces. It can be enjoyed on its own, added to salads, or paired with a yogurt‑herb sauce and fresh greens.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked spanakopita in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven to restore crispness. It can be frozen for up to 2 months if wrapped tightly in plastic.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy vegetable widely used in cooking. Cooked spinach is often added to soups, stews, casseroles and sauces. It has a tender texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and retains most of its nutrients after heat treatment.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach was known in ancient Rome and Greece, where it was used as a medicinal plant.
The iron content of spinach is often overstated: in raw form the iron is less bioavailable than in cooked spinach.
Spinach belongs to the amaranth family, along with beet and quinoa.
In the 1970s spinach became a staple of the "eat your greens" health movement in the United States.
There are several varieties of spinach – Savoy, Flat‑leaf and Semi‑Savoy – each with a different leaf texture.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Beta‑carotene in spinach converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immunity.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of protein and fiber
items.content: Helps maintain satiety and supports normal digestive function.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Like many vegetables, spinach may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing before cooking is recommended.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked spinach can be mixed into pasta, omelets, pizza, soups and smoothies. It is often sautéed briefly in a little oil or boiled for 2‑3 minutes to retain its bright green color.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh spinach in the refrigerator in an airtight container or bag with a paper towel to absorb excess moisture. Cooked spinach keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large poultry bird whose meat is high in protein and relatively low in fat, especially in the white breast portions. The drumstick is the dark thigh meat with skin, which stays juicy and flavorful after cooking. The skin is edible and provides beneficial fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is the national bird of the United States and is traditionally served on Thanksgiving.
Dark drumstick meat contains more iron and zinc than white breast meat.
Turkey skin is rich in collagen, which is good for skin and joint health.
Turkeys are often raised on free-range farms, which enhances flavor.
When properly cooked, the drumstick remains moist even without added fat.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked turkey drumstick provides about 29 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Dark turkey meat has less saturated fat than beef, making it a heart‑friendlier option.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The drumstick is abundant in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Turkey provides iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood health, immunity, and bone strength.

items.title: Collagen in the skin
items.content: Edible skin contains collagen that may benefit skin, hair, and nail health.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat or skin.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the drumstick is brined or seasoned with salt, sodium levels can be high; monitor intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Dark meat is relatively high in purines, which may be a concern for people with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey drumsticks can be roasted, pan‑fried, braised, or grilled. Keep the skin on during cooking to retain moisture, then eat it together with the meat. Serve with vegetables, sauces, or slice into salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw drumsticks in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked portions keep in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C for up to 4 months.
